chapter: Return to Atlanta and move north
title: Street dancing at Yates Drug Store and Ella B. Moore taking the money
summary: Green and the boys danced barefoot outside a drugstore in Augusta for coins; Ella B. Moore turned him upside down to shake out his pockets.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x:
Yeah. Yeah. I was the first one to leave, because I ran away. See, we had a falling out, you know. We used to was allowed to go out like for a walk or go out and play, you see. But I decided here going around where the people were, which we call white folks, you know. Let's go where the white folks is and maybe we can do some dancing and get them to throw us some money, you know.

And we used to go up front of a place in Augusta, Georgia, called Yates Drug Store, you know, and they had a sound system going too, playing music, and I could dance barefeet, you see, and we would get up in the light and start to dancing, you know, and attract the people's attention, customers going in and out of the store, and they would throw us nickels and dimes, you know, and quarters, half dollars.

And the money, they had money called the bow dollar then, you know.
And that's what we were trying to get, you know. Sometimes people would -- they would take and wrap the money up in --

some coins in maybe a dollar or five dollar bill or whatever, you know, and toss that at us, you know, because we had little comedies we'd do, like trying to pick up the money, you know. And we'd make the people laugh, and they'd throw more money, you see.

But that's how I had the falling out with Chinch and Ella B. Moore, because when we were coming home, she would ask us what we did, where had we been, you know, and, you know. And then she started asking us did we make any money. So I said, 'Well, now, I found a dime and a nickel, or something, you know, and reach in my pocket and try to pull the money out, say, see, -- you know how children are. She was saying, 'Is that all you got', you know? And I tried to, you know, tried to fib and say, yeah, that's it, you know. Oh, you got more than that, you know, and she grabbed me by my ankles, you know, and she turned me upside down. You understand? (Laughter) And shook all the moneys out of my pockets, you see. See, 'cause I used to like to buy candy and stuff, you know, and I'd say, well, you can't take all my money. I gave you the 15 cents, you know. You all got money, you know, trying to argue, you know, a child trying to argue with an adult, you know. Now, you mustn't tell a fib; you mustn't like, you

know, so just for that I'm going to keep all the money, you know. Okay, so I let it go. So a few times there she was -- I come to find out she was anxious for us to go out and play because, sure enough, see, Chuckles -- J. D. rather -- he was -- Slim, he was a great dancer. He was a great tap dancer, and that's really how the people, they enjoyed giving us money, you see.

What I wanted to do, I wanted to send the money back to my -- like my mother or something, you know, write a letter, because we had to write letters home, you see, wherever we was at, you know, in our handwriting, see, you know. But I never got a chance to do this, you see, and that's why I had the falling out.
